transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lina Huang (Redwood CSM); Rajesh Menon (CTO, CortexFleet), Emily Zhao (ML Eng), Aaron Blake (Infra Eng), Nora Feld (Product)
Links shared: https://redwood.internal/demo/edge-resilience (deck), drive: CORTEX-sample-traffic.csv

Auto-summary: quick walkthrough of API, Console, and Optimize features that address long prompt contexts and high-throughput streaming; demo shows graceful degradation to shorter context / fallback model, KV cache warmup, and backpressure metrics in console.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, I think we have about 45-50 minutes, so we'll go through a short deck and then Miguel will demo a couple of failure modes — long prompt sessions, TPS spikes and what happens when streaming starts lagging.

[00:22] Rajesh: Sounds good. We're especially worried about session handoff — we have multi-turn chat that can exceed 200k tokens across a session with lots of context. We want to make sure we don't silently drop prompts or hit hard timeouts for paying customers.

[00:40] Miguel: Totally, Rajesh. We'll show the KV cache behavior and how Redwood Optimize recommends quantization + batching to keep latency down. Quick note: some of my screenshots are the internal console — ignore path names.

[01:05] Emily: Quick qual question: are you demonstrating hosted only, or you'll show Dedicated and the private option? Data residency matters.

[01:17] Samira: We'll show hosted path first, then switch to a simulated Dedicated pool. The controls and APIs are the same; the difference is routing, reserved GPUs, and SLA.

[01:35] Nora: Also, how do you handle mid-session routing if capacity saturates — do you splice to a smaller model or queue? We can't have customers see huge latencies.

[01:50] Miguel: Great question. We route by policy: first try preferred model on low-latency pool, if capacity constrained we can either fall back to a compatible smaller quantized variant or route to a burst pool with a degraded latency SLO but preserved availability. For streaming specifically we also expose a per-connection backpressure signal — if the kernel queue grows past threshold we push a 429-style hint and the SDK can fallback to polling or shorter sequences.

[02:20] Aaron: That 429 hint — can it be noisy? Our infra auto-retries, might amplify load.

[02:32] Miguel: Yes, that's why we recommend client-side jitter and an exponential backoff with cap, and also a conservative retry policy in the SDK. We can also provide an explicit accept-throttle header so the client doesn't blindly requeue.

[03:00] Samira: Ok Miguel, can you kick off the first demo — long context, single session but lots of turns — and show the KV cache warmup and what happens when context crosses 65k tokens?

[03:18] Miguel: Sure — I'm going to run a session replay using the sample traffic you sent. Note: transcript may show slight ASR error where 'KV cache' becomes 'K V cash' in the recorded notes. Starting replay now.

[04:05] [DEMO - REPLAY START]
[04:10] Miguel: (typing) Sending first few messages, you can see in console the prefix cache warming — the hot-attention paths are filled, and per-call latency drops from ~420ms to ~160ms for the same seq length.

[04:45] Emily: Nice, is that with beam search or sampling?

[04:51] Miguel: Sampling with top-p 0.9; this workload is typical of chat. Next, I'm going to append longer system prompts so we cross into the 100k token region and watch how the runtime swaps contexts and what happens to streaming.

[05:25] Miguel: Now we hit truncation thresholds for the optimized kernels — the runtime will switch to chunked attention and we see a latency bump; console shows a 'context-mode: chunked' flag.

[05:50] Rajesh: Chunked attention — does that mean outputs are correct but slower? Any risk of token mismatch?

[05:58] Miguel: Correct — semantics preserved. We do extra cross-chunk aggregation, so it's slower. We also present an option to pin a pinned-KV store for very long-running sessions (this is a Dedicated feature) — that keeps latency competitive by persisting key/value caches across requests.

[06:25] Aaron: That pinned-KV — does it require a warmup period or is it instantaneous when session created?

[06:33] Miguel: There's a warmup (few requests) — we prefetch common prefixes. We can also snapshot a KV state after a training or curation step so you don't need to re-stream big context every time.

[07:00] [DEMO - STREAMING BACKPRESSURE SCENARIO]
[07:05] Miguel: I'm simulating a TPS spike — client floods with many concurrent sessions. Console now shows request queue depth rising, per-GPU outstanding tokens, and the backpressure gauge turning amber. At 2:37:55 in the trace (internal id) the SDK got a 'stream-lag' event and changed to poll fallback for a subset of connections.

[07:45] Nora: Where do you show that in the console? I want to surface that to the customer dashboard.

[07:53] Miguel: Under 'Routes -> Live Metrics' you'll see 'Streaming health' with backpressure events; you can set alerts for queue depth and average plugin latency. I'm toggling the chart to show 'client-side seen 429s' which correlate with the internal queue threshold.

[08:20] Emily: In our infra, we prefer graceful degradation to a shorter-context model rather than polling — does Redwood support switching to a smaller model mid-session preserving the last N tokens?

[08:33] Miguel: Yes — we have a 'context-aware fallback' policy where the router will drop oldest messages beyond retention and continue with a lower-capacity but latency-optimized model. The console's rollout API can orchestrate that as a canary then global.

[09:05] Rajesh: What's the observable for 'dropped context' vs 'truncated context' so we can SRE-alarm appropriately?

[09:12] Miguel: We emit an event 'context_truncation' with the size dropped and reason; also a 'fallback_model' event. Both are visible in the trace and can be piped to your SIEM / Splunk.

[09:40] Samira: Let's walk through a timeout example — Aaron, could you ask the typical infra question on how we'd detect and mitigate a 30s streaming stall?

[09:53] Aaron: Sure. If a streaming connection stalls for 30s, does Redwood keep the execution in memory or does it GC state? How do we avoid ghost sessions eating up memory?

[10:08] Miguel: We have configurable idle timeouts. By default, streaming connections with no client ACK for 20s are considered 'stalled' and put into a transient queue with reduced resources; after a longer threshold (default 2 minutes) we snapshot state and evict memory. For Dedicated, you can increase those thresholds. We also persist KV snapshots to avoid recompute on resume.

[10:45] Emily: Any chance client-side TLS or proxies cause false stalls? We've seen proxies buffer a chunk and then flush.

[10:52] Miguel: Definitely — we recommend using our SDK which implements low-level keepalives and chunking to avoid proxy buffering. We can also switch to an HTTP fallback with shorter polling intervals in proxy-prone networks.

[11:20] [DEMO - TIMERS AND CIRCUITS]
[11:24] Miguel: I'm toggling the circuit-breaker to simulate repeated failures for a route; console shows automatic route-level ramp-down and triggers a model fallback. You can configure the circuit sensitivity per-customer.

[11:55] Nora: Are these circuit breakers per model or per route? We have a global route that hits many models.

[12:03] Miguel: They're per-route by default but can be aggregated across models. For your global route we suggest a two-layer policy: route-level thresholds + model-level fallback.

[12:30] Samira: Quick pause — any compliance/security questions before we show the Optimize recommendations?

[12:39] Rajesh: We need to ensure audit logs for all fallbacks and token-level cost attributions are available for billing. Also SOC2 and KMS integration for Dedicated.

[12:52] Samira: We'll include SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up pack. Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS; logs are exportable to CloudWatch/Splunk.

[13:10] [DEMO - OPTIMIZE SUGGESTIONS]
[13:15] Miguel: Now the Optimize tool — it analyzed your sample traffic and suggests: 1) quantize to int8 for the mid-ctx model, 2) set max_batch_size=64 for short-turn chats, 3) enable prefix KV caching for long sessions and pin for premium users. Each suggestion has an estimated cost delta in the console.

[13:50] Emily: Those cost deltas are approximations — how accurate are they? We charge back exact token costs to product lines.

[13:56] Miguel: The estimates are based on our per-token microbenchmarks and your sample distribution; we hedge with conservative margins. For final billing you'd get exact token usage export and per-token attribution.

[14:20] Rajesh: We need to model a high TPS scenario — roughly 2k concurrent short sessions with 20 RPS each for short bursts. How would Redwood behave?

[14:33] Miguel: For bursts we recommend a hybrid policy: reserved capacity for the base 1k concurrent and an autoscaled burst pool up to 3k. The router will spill to cheaper region pools if cross-region capacity is available. Also, TTL-based cache warmers reduce the initial cold-start cost.

[15:00] Aaron: How does quantization interact with long-context chunking? Any loss in correctness for aggregations?

[15:08] Miguel: Good point — quantization mainly affects weight storage and kernel precision; chunked attention still computes aggregation in FP16/FP32 paths when necessary. Optimize will flag potential quality regressions with a scoring metric tied to your eval prompts.

[15:45] [DEMO - LIVE FAULT INJECTION]
[15:50] Miguel: I'm injecting intermittent GPU slowdowns on one node to show routing fallback. Watch the route: we see increased p95 latency then an automatic shave to the fallback pool and a canary increment.

[16:20] Nora: Can that happen without an obvious outage to customers?

[16:26] Miguel: Yes — the goal is graceful degradation so customers see slightly higher latency or shorter responses rather than 5xx errors. We also surface a 'degraded' health status in the customer dashboard.

[16:55] Emily: For billing alignment, when you fallback to smaller model do you bill at the smaller model rate, or the original?

[17:05] Samira: We bill based on the model actually executed. If router falls back to a smaller model, that's charged accordingly. For some enterprise deals we can set committed price bands for fallbacks.

[17:25] Rajesh: Security again — if you snapshot KV to persistent store, is that encrypted with our KMS?

[17:31] Miguel: Yes, we support customer KMS and HSM-backed keys for Dedicated. Snapshots are encrypted at rest and access is audited.

[18:00] [QUESTION from Aaron] Aaron: Are there any known streaming edge cases with egress cost explosion if we fall back and retry loops?

[18:12] Miguel: Retry storms can amplify costs; we mitigate with server-side retry caps, idempotency tokens, and backpressure signals. The Optimize tool will flag policies that risk retry amplification.

[18:38] Samira: Let's do a quick walkthrough of the Console's tracing for a sample failing session. Miguel, bring up a recorded trace where a session hit a 30s stall and recovered by polling.

[18:50] Miguel: (shares trace) Here you see timeline: stream start, large payload, queue spike, 'stream-lag' event, SDK switched to poll after 21s, resumed after checkpoint, then finalization. The trace includes event tags we can map to your alerting.

[19:25] Emily: Can we export these events to our observability?

[19:28] Miguel: Yes — events can be shipped via webhook, Kafka, or direct S3 export.

[19:45] [INTERMISSION - CUSTOMER CHALLENGES]
[19:50] Rajesh: A few constraints — we have GDPR concerns for EU users, so routing to non-EU regions requires consent. Also we have limits on per-tenant storage for KV snapshots.

[20:08] Samira: For GDPR we support region pinning and data residency; KV snapshot retention is configurable per-customer. We'll document defaults and per-tenant overrides.

[20:35] Nora: On dev side we think it's critical to have test harness for long-context regressions so we don't ship a rollout that increases hallucination. Is there an eval integration?

[20:46] Miguel: Definitely — Optimize integrates with eval sets and will do regression comparisons when you change quantization or rollout a fallback model. You can attach a prompt set and automated quality alerts.

[21:10] Emily: This is great. Can we talk about the Dedicated pilot timeline? We want to run a 2-week pilot with 1-2 reserved nodes and a burst policy.

[21:22] Samira: Yes, generally we do a 2-4 week pilot. For the reserved nodes we provision a Dedicated pool with a canary config and run your sample traffic overnight to calibrate batch sizes and prefix caching.

[21:40] Rajesh: Pricing — baseline plus reserved capacity. We need a one-page cost estimate.

[21:47] Samira: I'll send a preliminary pricing sheet after the call. We'll include committed hours and an engineering support add-on for the pilot.

[22:05] [DEEP TECH Q&A]
[22:10] Aaron: On the kernel selection — you mentioned runtime picks kernels by seq length distribution. If we have mixed short and ultra-long sessions, do you fragment models or keep separate pools?

[22:22] Miguel: We use heterogeneous pools: short-seq optimized GPUs and long-seq tuned nodes. Router tags requests and sends them to the appropriate pool. You can pin specific user segments to a pool to avoid noisy neighbor problems.

[22:45] Emily: Can we do per-tenant quotas limiting total in-flight tokens to protect costs?

[22:53] Miguel: Yes — per-tenant token caps, rate limits, and route-specific budgets are configurable and enforced by the router.

[23:15] Rajesh: Any hidden gotchas with SDKs and proxies?

[23:20] Miguel: Watch out for HTTP proxies that buffer chunked responses; use the SDK's keepalive or fallback to HTTP polling. Also, long websockets may be killed by intermediate devices; we suggest health pings.

[23:50] Samira: We're about halfway through — Miguel, can you show the Optimize results for our sample traffic that recommend batching tweaks?

[23:58] Miguel: Sure — Optimize suggests: short-turns batch=32, mid-turns batch=16, long-turns batch=4 and dynamic batching with latency SLO target 200ms. The console sim shows predicted p50/p95.

[24:30] Emily: If we enforce 200ms p95, do we lose throughput? What's the tradeoff curve?

[24:36] Miguel: There's always a tradeoff. Optimize computes a Pareto curve — you pick a p95 target and it returns expected throughput and cost. For example, at p95 200ms we estimate 40% higher CPU/GPU usage vs 300ms p95.

[25:05] [SIMULATED FAILURE - NETWORK PARTITION]
[25:10] Miguel: Injecting network partition to a region; you'll see capacity reroute to fallback regions. Notice the console annotation where we mark the 'partial outage' and the router automatically opens more burst capacity elsewhere.

[25:40] Nora: How do you handle data residency in that case? We can't route EU users to US regions during a GDPR event.

[25:48] Miguel: We honor region policies — if region pinning is enabled, the router will not reroute across pinned regions; instead it will shift load within region or present an overload signal.

[26:10] Rajesh: For the pilot, we'd like explicit logs for fallback reasons per request. Is that available?

[26:17] Miguel: Yes — every decision is annotated in the request trace with reason codes like 'capacity', 'latency', 'policy-pin', etc.

[26:40] [END-TO-END TRACE WALKTHROUGH]
[26:45] Miguel: Walkthrough showing a request that spanned multiple fallbacks and ended in a truncated context but preserved intent. You can see the event stream of 'fallback_model: small-v2', 'context_truncation: 420tokens', 'client-retry: suppressed'.

[27:15] Emily: Will the Optimize alerts notify product teams when model rollouts cause quality regressions?

[27:22] Miguel: Yes — you can bind eval dashboards to product webhooks to trigger rollbacks if metrics cross thresholds.

[27:45] Rajesh: Anything else we should be aware of before pilot? Limitations?

[27:52] Miguel: A few caveats: persistently tail-latency sensitive workloads may need dedicated long-seq nodes; quantization can sometimes show small quality regressions that we flag; and proxy-induced buffering is the most common cause of streaming anomalies.

[28:15] Samira: Great. Quick recap and next steps — Samira to send pricing and SOC2 docs, Miguel to hand over runbook and benchmark script, Rajesh to send traffic sample and acceptance criteria. We've captured those in action items.

[28:35] Rajesh: Timeline — aiming to start pilot week of March 16th.

[28:42] Samira: We'll target that. Any final quick questions?

[28:47] Nora: One last: how do you measure hallucination/regression in Optimize?

[28:53] Miguel: We use automated eval sets plus fuzz testing; Optimize computes a quality delta and flags prompts with metric drop > threshold. You can also attach human review flows.

[29:20] Emily: Can you share the demo artifacts and the precise Optimize config you used?

[29:25] Samira: Yes — I'll include the Optimize snapshot and the console screenshots in the follow-up zip.

[29:40] [CLOSING]
[29:45] Samira: Thanks everyone, appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the docs and the pricing. Miguel and Lina will be on the pilot kick-off.

[30:00] Rajesh: Thank you, Samira. Looking forward to the pilot.

[30:08] Emily: Thanks all.

[30:15] Miguel: Thanks, talk soon.

[30:20] (call ends)

Notes: transcript has occasional ASR artifacts. The demo included internal trace ids and screenshots; links and artifacts to be shared off-channel.
